http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/12/libya.text: The head of military intelligence for the Libyan National Army (LNA) led by Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar has been killed in a car bombing in Benghazi, authorities confirmed on Tuesday.Fawzi al-Mansouri was assassinated on Monday when an explosive stuck to his car detonated as he was leaving a local mosque at night, the statement said.Al-Mansouri was a senior figure within the LNA's intelligence apparatus and had close ties to the Haftar family.He played a key role in the LNA's campaign against jihadist groups, including the so-called Islamic State group (IS), between 2014 and 2017 in eastern Libya.Al-Mansouri, whom the LNA described as a "heroic martyr," was also a leading figure during Haftar's 2019 offensive to seize the capital Tripoli in an operation backed by Russia and Egypt.Haftar's offensive was eventually beaten back by forces loyal to the Tripoli government, which was in turn supported by Turkey.Khaled Haftar, the son of Khalifa and LNA's chief of the general staff, said in a statement that an investigation was opened, adding that "indicators point to a despicable terrorist tactic"."Terrorism is a project targeting the entire region, not just Libya," the statement added.The bombing was a setback to efforts by the Haftars to paint a picture of stability in the areas they control."An attack of this sophistication in an LNA stronghold is also a major blow to the group's security credentials," analyst with UK-based Verisk Maplecroft Hamish Kinnear said."The intelligence required to target such a high-profile figure successfully is indicative of significant capabilities on the part of the responsible actor," Kinnear added.Authorities have yet to identify the perpetrators.Tripoli government condemns 'terrorist attack'Libya has been split between rival administrations since NATO's intervention helped topple Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.Two governments are currently vying for power: the UN-recognised administration in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, and a rival administration in Benghazi backed by the elder Haftar, who is considered the de facto ruler.Dbeibah has governed since 2021 following a UN-brokered political agreement but without a fresh electoral mandate, as a planned December 2021 election was cancelled amid disputes over candidate eligibility and the legal basis for the vote.His government has faced sustained domestic opposition, including protests in Tripoli earlier this year over electricity cuts.A former Gaddafi general and close ally who defected and lived in the US for nearly two decades before returning to Libya after 2011, Haftar built the LNA into the main force in the east and south.The Tripoli-based government issued a statement denouncing a "terrorist attack" against al-Mansouri, saying it condemned the killing "regardless of one party's positions or alliances".Khaled's office later said in a statement that authorities arrested a "terrorist cell in Benghazi that was preparing to carry out acts of sabotage" but did not say whether it was linked with al-Mansouri's killing.Authorities in Benghazi held al-Mansouri's funeral on Tuesday afternoon, publishing photos that showed armed men in military fatigues with the attendance of senior LNA officials at the ceremony, including Khaled and Saddam Haftar.In a statement, the LNA said it would "not cease fighting terrorism and will continue our struggle for the stability and security of Libya, as well as for the unification of its institutions".US wants Saddam to take over Libya?Libya holds Africa's largest proven oil reserves, which have fuelled both sides of the political divide.Yet efforts remain under way to unify the country's executive powers under a Washington-mediated plan that the LNA has publicly backed.Under the leaked terms of the plan, Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah would remain in charge of the Tripoli-based government while Lieutenant General Saddam Haftar — also Khalifa's son — would be elevated to a senior national executive role, possibly heading a unified presidential structure.Saddam Haftar was appointed deputy commander-in-chief of the LNA in August 2025 as part of a restructuring that effectively distributed operational command among Khalifa's main heirs."None of this bodes well for a US plan to re-unify Libya," Kinnear said, adding that under the roadmap, neither side "is likely to be satisfied with their respective positions for long"."A new, destabilising power struggle could soon emerge."Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui said the killing would "disrupt, or at the very least delay" the US-brokered deal."The agreement rests on two premises: that security reigns supreme in Benghazi, and that for senior officers, loyalty to Saddam (Haftar's son and heir apparent) guarantees protection in the Benghazi stronghold," Harchaoui explained.But "a bomb that kills the head of military intelligence as he leaves a mosque undermines these premises," he said.Meanwhile, reunification would "require some gestures of openness toward reform and change within the army", Harchaoui concluded.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/09/06/irani.text: Iran said on Sunday that its forces had targeted a US naval drone as it attempted to enter the Strait of Hormuz, as tensions in the region escalate once again.In a statement shared by state TV, the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said it had launched an attack on an "unmanned surface vessel" off the south coast of Iran as it was about to enter the strategic waterway.“The aggressor United States must understand that it has no choice but to leave the region and stop its acts of mischief,” the statement read.It comes after the IRGC said it had also carried out strikes on three oil tankers and three US-linked vessels in the Strait.The force has also warned ships against attempts to navigate the passage - a crucial oil and gas transit chokepoint - through unapproved routes.The incidents are the latest flashpoints in renewed confrontation between the two nations.On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that its forces had struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to what it said were ballistic missile strikes launched by the IRGC against two navy warships."Following Iran’s failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask," it said in a statement. "American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo (also known as the “Noxen”) in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship"."A U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer successfully evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks. No American personnel were harmed," it added.CENTCOM has also shared video footage on social media appearing to show the strikes.The conflict reignited last Sunday after US forces targeted Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz.The IRGC later confirmed strikes had hit Larak Island, before launching retaliatory attacks on US bases across the Middle East.On Saturday, Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of CENTCOM, issued a warning to Tehran and its oil fleet in the wake of the strikes."Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours. We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet," he said.

https://www.wglt.org/2026-09-16/doj-char.text: Sign In Sign In On Air Now Playing WGLT DOJ charges Russian agents with plotting attacks, including in the U.S. NPR | By Ryan Lucas Published September 16, 2026 at 12:19 PM CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche delivers remarks during a press briefing in the Rose Garden of the White House on Tuesday. The Justice Department has brought charges against five suspected Russian intelligence operatives for allegedly plotting attacks against the Kremlin's perceived enemies around the world, including the murder-for-hire of at least one prominent dissident in the U.S. The indictment, which was unsealed in federal court in Manhattan, says the defendants belong to a network that "is one arm of the Russian Federation's apparatus used to carry out external attacks, including murder, around the world." The network also allegedly conducted operations against civilian and military targets in European allies of Ukraine. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the two countries have been locked in a bloody war since then. Several European allies of Ukraine, including Poland, Germany and Czechia, have accused Russia of conducting sabotage attacks on their soil in recent years. Now, the U.S. is making similar allegations in a criminal indictment against specific, alleged Russian operatives. "It is our job to stop America's adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil," Attorney General Todd Blanche said. "And that's precisely what we are doing thanks to the work of the FBI and our Justice Department prosecutors." Court papers identify two of the defendants as Yuri Khrameev, a former colonel in the Russian intelligence service, and his son, Kirill Khrameev, who is a suspected officer in Russia's FSB intelligence agency. The other defendants are Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, both from Cuba, and Angel Eduardo Castro, who is from Venezuela. Prosecutors say all three men live in Russia. The five defendants are charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, while Yuri Khrameev, Suarez and Castro also face one count of murder-for-hire conspiracy. Officials say all of the defendants remain at large. Venezuelan alleged to seek murder of Russian dissident The indictment paints a detailed picture of the defendants' alleged efforts since 2024 to recruit and carry out a series of targeted killings and acts of sabotage on behalf of the Russian government. One of the alleged plots took place between July and August 2026, when prosecutors say the network recruited a Venezuelan citizen, identified only as U.S. Resident 1, living in Brooklyn to surveil and murder a prominent Russian dissident in the U.S. The dissident is not named in court papers. Prosecutors say Castro and Suarez used an encrypted messaging app to communicate with U.S. Resident 1, and gave him two addresses to surveil that were associated with the dissident. They also provided detailed instructions on how to take photos and videos of the locations. Suarez allegedly stated the addresses were associated with someone they "want to eliminate they want to disappear," and offered $40,000 "for whoever does the work." U.S. Resident 1 said he was willing to take photos and videos but not commit murder. The indictment says Suarez then asked U.S. Resident 1 if he knew "someone who wants to do construction," which prosecutors say was code for "carrying out the murder." Suarez allegedly stated that he was under pressure from his boss to get the job done. He also said that he had a team in Mexico who could do it but that they weren't immediately available. U.S. citizen allegedly recruited in Lithuania The indictment also chronicles a separate alleged plot in Europe in 2025 involving efforts to recruit a U.S. citizen to surveil and murder a Kremlin critic believed to be living in Vilnius, Lithuania. In late June 2025, prosecutors say, the American met with Kirill Khrameev at the Estonia-Russia border, where Khrameev offered to pay the American, who is not named, to take photos of an address in Vilnius. The American then kept in touch via an encrypted messaging app with Yuri Khrameev, who told him he needed to send photos or videos of the target's residence every two to three days, according to the indictment. Court papers say Yuri Khrameev told the American that the individual was being targeted for "spreading dirt" about Russia and "telling the media and the common people that the Russians are the aggressors." The indictment says the American was offered $25,000 to carry out the murder, which Khrameev said could be conducted by "throwing a bottle of gasoline" or "sticking a knife" in the victim, but the American declined, fearing he would easily be caught. Yuri Khrameev then offered him a "simpler job," such as setting fire to a warehouse or electrical substation, according to prosecutors. "I am interested in all the countries that are helping Ukraine," Khrameev allegedly wrote the American, adding that he was interested in targeting "military facilities and dual-use facilities… located in the countries of the NATO military bloc." "Serious money for serious work" "I'm offering serious money for serious work," he allegedly added. The indictment appears to include details related to some other countries' allegations of Russian sabotage. It says that Durruthy, one of the Cubans, played a role in coordinating travel and payment for terrorist acts, including in Prague. The indictment says he transferred more than $1,000 in cryptocurrency to a "criminal associate" and booked hotels in the Czech Republic and in Poland for the associate. The indictment includes a photo pulled from an online account associated with Durruthy that prosecutors say appears to show potential attack sites in the Polish capital. https://aa.com.tr/en/eurasia/explainer-h.text: World Russia-Ukraine War Eurasia Features EXPLAINER - How has Russia-Ukraine fighting intensified since September? Russia has expanded missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure over past month, including ports, while Ukraine has stepped up long-range strikes on Russian energy and logistics sites Burc Eruygur 09 October 2026 • Update : 09 October 2026 ISTANBUL Russia and Ukraine claim that targeting of infrastructure is linked to military and military-related activities while countries accuse each other of endangering or killing civilians Tensions extend beyond Ukraine, with Russia’s westernmost exclave of Kaliningrad adding to friction between Moscow and Europe Fighting between Russia and Ukraine has intensified since early last month, with attacks increasing in both frequency and scope. Russia has stepped up attacks targeting Ukraine’s railways, bridges, port infrastructure, electricity facilities and transport hubs, including sites close to the Polish border and in the capital Kyiv. Ukraine, meanwhile, has intensified attacks deep inside Russia, hitting oil refineries and fuel infrastructure as well as military airfields and air-defense systems. Both countries deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities. Amid the surge in strikes, tensions between Russia and NATO have also increased, particularly around the Baltic Sea, with Moscow warning NATO that Russia was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the alliance attempted to isolate its westernmost exclave of Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia. Russian strikes in Ukraine Since early September, Russian strikes in Ukraine have killed and injured many people while also damaging local infrastructure in multiple regions, according to reports, including by Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. Among the reported targets of such strikes were a border checkpoint with Romania on Sept. 6 as well as the building of the My-Ukraina TV channel, part of the country’s United News telethon, on Sept. 8. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of carrying out “demonstrative strikes” on airports near the country's capital ahead of a planned visit to Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The Sept. 6 trip marked Witkoff and Kushner's first visit to Ukraine since US-mediated peace negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv began. Apart from Kyiv, other Ukrainian regions have also been the target of Russian airstrikes, most notably the southern region of Odesa, where infrastructure and vessels approaching Ukrainian ports have been hit. On Sept. 12, Ukrainian authorities said at least 48 people were injured following Russian strikes in the region, which Zelenskyy said also hit a hotel in the port city of Chornomorsk. The Russian Defense Ministry, meanwhile, claimed it hit port infrastructure facilities at the port of Chornomorsk that were “used for unloading and storing military supplies” as well as two dry-cargo vessels and a sea tugboat during overnight strikes. Railway infrastructure has also been targeted by Russian strikes, with one of the most notable incidents occurring on Sept. 14, when a Warsaw-bound train was hit by a drone near the Ukrainian-Polish border in the Volyn region. Ukraine claimed that the Russian drone was likely targeting a diplomatic train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European officials which had left the station before the strike. Moscow said later that day it was continuing to target railway infrastructure facilities in western Ukraine that were “used for transporting military cargo from European countries.” Ukrainian strikes in Russia During the same period, Russia reported extensively on Ukrainian strikes, particularly targeting the energy sector. Local authorities reported continued strikes on Russian logistics centers, including on Sept. 11, when a drone attack hit facilities belonging to online retailer Ozon. Ukraine has intensified drone strikes on Russian logistics facilities in a campaign that began in mid-July and has spread across several Russian regions. Since July, Ukrainian drones have targeted logistics centers of Russia's largest e-commerce retailer Wildberries in multiple regions, and strikes have expanded to facilities belonging to Ozon since August. Kyiv has alleged that both retailers are playing a role in Russia’s military supply chain, while Moscow and the two companies maintain that the facilities are commercial. Ukrainian strikes have also continued to target energy facilities across several Russian regions, including the Novorossiysk oil terminal in the southern Krasnodar region and facilities at the port of Ust-Luga in the northwestern Leningrad region. The sustained attacks have constrained Russia's ability to process crude into transportation fuels. In response, Russia introduced diesel export curbs in July and extended them through September. US President Donald Trump urged Zelenskyy in mid-September to halt military strikes against Russian diesel refineries, warning that the operations are creating global fuel shortages. Russia also accused Ukraine of attempting to disrupt its Sept. 18-20 parliamentary elections, during which it said Kyiv targeted local infrastructure, including polling stations. Ukraine did not comment on the accusation. Kaliningrad tensions The escalation amid the ongoing war in Ukraine has also become increasingly visible beyond the war-torn country due to rhetoric surrounding Russia's Kaliningrad region. A Russian semi-exclave bordered by Lithuania to the north and east, Poland to the south, and the Baltic Sea to the west and northwest, the Kaliningrad region has captured media attention after some Russian diplomatic missions in Europe warned that Moscow would use "all weapons" in its arsenal to defend its territory, including nuclear arms. "Those advocating plans to blockade or strike Kaliningrad should have no illusions about the consequences. Any British or NATO military action against Russian territory would be met with a response using all means at Russia’s disposal, including nuclear weapons," the Russian Embassy in the UK said on Sept. 29. At a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin also said that any direct attack on Russia or attempt to annex the exclave would inevitably raise the issue of using "all weapons and means at Moscow’s disposal." Putin's remarks came after reports that Russia had sent a letter to NATO reiterating Moscow's position concerning the Kaliningrad region. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte did not disclose the contents of the letter but told journalists on Sept. 30 that the organization had responded. “We are a defensive alliance,” he said, calling on Russia to "stop the nuclear threats" and “stop the war in Ukraine.” news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription contact_the_ombudsman is_there_an_error_in_this_story LATEST NEWS All Anthropic security official warns of worsening cyber threats, risks to critical infrastructure Brazil electoral prosecutors seek to fine Meta over alleged breach of candidate equality orders Thousands protest in Vienna over education budget cuts Trump invokes Defense Production Act to boost US oil production Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted 11 Houthi drones and a ballistic missile Britain’s defense chief urges public to prepare for cyberattack-driven supply chain disruptions Kenya launches emergency aid efforts as hundreds flee deadly clashes in Ethiopia See All First poll since Brazil’s first round presidential election predicts Flavio 53%, Lula 47% in upcoming runoff US immigration agent shoots man in New York City

https://tibet.net/sikyong-penpa-tsering-.text: Sikyong Penpa Tsering Wraps Up Official Engagements in the Czech Republic with Media Outreach 2 weeks ago Subscribe Views: 7,339 Sikyong Penpa Tsering Wraps Up Official Engagements in the Czech Republic with Media Outreach Prague, Czech Republic: On 14 October 2026, the concluding day of his official engagements around the Forum 2000 Conference in Prague, Sikyong Penpa Tsering of the Central Tibetan Administration focused his outreach on prominent Czech national media to amplify global awareness of Tibet’s human rights, religious freedom, and geopolitical situation. The morning commenced with an in-depth television interview with Dana Zlatohlávková of Czech Television (Česká televize), the nation’s public broadcaster, held at the Holiday Inn Prague. During the interview, Sikyong reflected on the enduring moral bond between Václav Havel and His Holiness the Dalai Lama while expressing gratitude to the Czech leadership and public for their steadfast solidarity. He reaffirmed that the reincarnation of His Holiness the Dalai Lama is governed solely by His Holiness and the Gaden Phodrang Trust, condemning Beijing’s attempts to appoint a successor as an absurd political tool and asserting that the next Dalai Lama will be born in a free world. Sikyong also sounded alarms over China’s accelerated assimilation policies under the guise of “Ethnic Unity and Progress” laws—calling them a legal cover for cultural genocide through colonial boarding schools, language suppression, and pervasive surveillance—while reiterating the CTA’s firm commitment to the Middle Way Approach in seeking genuine autonomy and holding onto hope for future dialogue with a sensible Chinese leadership. Following the broadcast, Sikyong held an extensive media interaction with Magdalena Slezáková from Deník N, one of the Czech Republic’s leading independent daily newspapers. During the interview, Sikyong cautioned that Beijing’s domestic repression in Tibet serves as a blueprint for its global ambitions, urging democratic nations to resist Chinese economic coercion. Drawing on Václav Havel’s legacy and the principle of impermanence, Sikyong described the Chinese Communist Party as a primary enabler of global authoritarianism that exploits Tibet’s fragile ecology and exports surveillance technology. Reaffirming the CTA’s commitment to the Middle Way Approach, he called on world leaders to abandon short-term political complacency, address trade imbalances, and unite to protect democratic freedoms against unchecked Chinese hegemony. Following the successful completion of his official engagements in Prague, Sikyong headed to Berlin. En route, Sikyong visited Lány Chateau (Zámek Lány), the summer residence of the Czech President, where he was received by Alexandr Neuman, personal secretary to the late former President Václav Havel. In commemoration of what would have been President Havel’s 90th birth anniversary this year, Alexandr guided Sikyong on a tour around the historic residence, reflecting on fond memories and the deep, enduring friendship shared between His Holiness the Dalai Lama and President Václav Havel. Upon arrival in Berlin, Germany, Sikyong Penpa Tsering was warmly welcomed by representatives and members of the Tibetan Community in Germany. Throughout the day’s proceedings, Sikyong was accompanied by Representative Thinlay Chukki of the Tibet Bureau Geneva, who assisted in coordinating the engagements.
